subject: to mshape or to not mshape

messages.author: a0f8ae60bd31a713
messages.subject: to mshape or to not mshape
parts:
Dear all,

 

I’m analysing stomata from an evergreen tree species along and altitudinal gradient. So far, I have collected 2D landmarks for 320 stomata (32 leaves, 10 stomata per leaf). 

I have already performed simple allometry model and evaluate HOS converting altitude to a three-way factor (low, middle and high). Both Csize and faltitude seem to have a significant effect in the shape variation of stomata, and altitude groups have common allometry. However, I’m unsure if it would be better idea running the analysis based on mshape of stomata per leaf within altitude groups, mainly because I have measure 10 stomata (replicates) per leaf, and perhaps, I could use it to understand stomatal shape variation within leaves or measurement error.

I would also like to incorporate in my analysis other variables I have measured such as, mean stomatal density, mean stomatal index, mean leaf area, and environmental variables (e.g. mean annual temperature). and here, I think, is where the mshape of  per leaf could come in handy. Any advice will be greatly appreciate.


Thanks in advance,


Giselle

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] to mshape or to not mshape
parts:
Giselle,

You have to be careful because you also probably have size variation among stomata both within and across leaves that you do not want to disregard when finding means.  I would recommend - because common allometry can be assumed - that you find allometry-free shapes before getting means.  Here is an example for how to do that:

res <- prcoD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize), data = mydata, iter = 1)$residuals # removing allometry
means <- prcoD.lm(coords ~ 1, data = mydata, iter = 1)$fitted # overall mean shape
Y.adj <- mean + res # These are shapes with allometry removed
mydata$coords.adj <- arrayspecs(Y.adj, p, k) # using p = number of landmarks and k = 2 for 2D data

Then you could use mshape by leaf to get leaf mean shapes on coords.adj.  This way, if you have a leaf with many large stomata or many small stomata, you are estimating the mean shape of the leaf as if it has the average sized stomata, like all other leaves.

I agree that the leaf is a better research subject than the individual, repeated measures on each leaf.

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.author: 511e44c7d1e1bab0
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] to mshape or to not mshape
parts:
Giselle,

just an addition to what Mike said: if you are interested in also looking at within-leaf variation, and maybe contrasting it to across-leaf variation, you will might consider (before or after size correction, or both, that is a matter of what exactly you want to see) running a model with leaf (I mean the individual from which you sampled 10 stomata) as a random factor.

Good resources for how to set this up in procD.lm (which is basically now fully based on lm.rrpp) are the help file of the function, the help file of lm.rrpp and Mike´s vignette from the last big update of geomorph, i.e.: vignette("geomorph.assistance")

Cheers,

Antigoni

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] to mshape or to not mshape
parts:
Hi Giselle,

Your interpretation below is correct.  On average, despite much shape variation of stomata within leaves, you observe an altitude effect to change stomata shapes in some way.

One thing you might also consider doing is comparing leaf shape disparity - the shape variances - among altitudinal levels.  Maybe you see more variation in shape in one place compared to another.

Cheers!
Mike

Hi Mike,

On Fri, 19 Jul 2019 at 05:06, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Giselle,

Your interpretation below is correct.  On average, despite much shape variation of stomata within leaves, you observe an altitude effect to change stomata shapes in some way.

One thing you might also consider doing is comparing leaf shape disparity - the shape variances - among altitudinal levels.  Maybe you see more variation in shape in one place compared to another.

Cheers!
